Ophthalmology · published research

Myopia

Multiple pediatric trials report slower axial elongation and refractive progression with repeated low-level red light, but effects vary by protocol and follow-up. Long-term safety and rebound remain uncertain.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Multiple pediatric trials report slower axial elongation and refractive progression with repeated low-level red light, but effects vary by protocol and follow-up. Long-term safety and rebound remain uncertain.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact myopia category contains 155 unique publication titles. Records include clinical trials, observational studies, secondary analyses, reviews, meta-analyses, protocols, and animal or laboratory models; publication count is not cohort count. Human reports include 28 records tagged as randomized trials, with many follow-up or secondary papers that may reuse participants. Deng et al. 2024

Human and clinical evidence

The clinical literature is predominantly pediatric and focuses on repeated low-level red-light therapy for slowing axial elongation and refractive progression. Randomized comparisons and pooled reviews report a favorable short-term signal versus control or some alternative treatments. A 2024 one-year randomized trial of daily 650 nm light reported less progression in spherical-equivalent refraction and axial length, while the authors called for independent replication and longer follow-up. Results are not uniform across devices, treatment frequency, baseline myopia, and comparator. Reports of axial shortening, post-trial follow-up, and structural retinal measures require separate interpretation rather than being counted as independent cohorts. Cao et al. 2024

Animal evidence

The source includes chick, guinea-pig, tree-shrew, mouse, and other experimental work on refractive development and wavelength effects. These studies inform mechanisms but do not establish pediatric clinical effectiveness or safety.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Cell studies and retinal or choroidal imaging analyses examine mechanisms and safety markers.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols vary in wavelength, power, duration, frequency, device geometry, and whether treatment is combined with orthokeratology or defocus lenses. Most clinical records come from East Asian populations, with more recent studies in other regions. Results from one device and adherence pattern should not be generalized automatically to all red-light products.

Interpretation

There is a substantial and growing short-term clinical evidence base for pediatric myopia control, but publication totals overstate independent cohorts. Rebound after stopping, rare retinal effects, and long-term visual safety remain important uncertainties. Larger independent trials with transparent device dosimetry and extended follow-up are needed.

Publications and records155 unique publication titles: 83 human-tagged records, including 28 tagged randomized trials, 6 non-randomized records, and 2 case series; the source also tags 24 reviews, 22 meta-analyses, 2 systematic reviews, 2 protocols, and preclinical studies.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The source category contains many pediatric trials and observational reports, along with reviews, meta-analyses, and preclinical studies. Randomized evidence suggests short-term slowing of axial elongation and refractive progression, but protocols and populations vary. Follow-up publications may share cohorts, and long-term safety and rebound remain active questions.
